title: Elizabeth of Portugal (4 July)
hook: a queen who rode between armies to make peace

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thomas, the doubter who said my Lord and my God. That was your line. What did you stay in the room long enough to see? Day one thousand six.

Two armies face each other across a field. On one side, a king. On the other, his own son, who has risen against him. Banners, horses, men waiting for the signal. And then, tradition says, a woman on a mule rides out alone into the open ground between them. She is the king's wife and the rebel's mother. She stops there and will not move until they talk. Today, the queen in the middle. Elizabeth of Portugal.
screen: `TWO ARMIES ACROSS A FIELD.` → `A FATHER AND HIS SON.` → `A QUEEN RIDES INTO THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Elizabeth was a princess of Aragon, in Spain, married young to King Denis of Portugal. The marriage was not easy. Denis was a capable king, and an unfaithful husband. Elizabeth's lives tell of her raising his children by other women alongside her own, and of a quiet, stubborn life of prayer and care for the poor in the middle of a royal court. In public, her work was peace. When her son Afonso rose against his father, the kingdom came close to war between them. Elizabeth went back and forth, pleading with each, and on at least one occasion, tradition says, she rode between the two armies to stop the battle before it began. She also helped settle quarrels between Portugal and its neighbors. Jesus says it in the Sermon on the Mount. In the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." Notice what a peacemaker in this story actually does. Not a speech from a safe distance. She puts her own body in the gap. She loves both sides too much to let either win by killing the other. There's also a gentler legend about her. Tradition says she was carrying bread to the poor in her cloak when the king stopped her and asked what she had. She opened the cloak, and it was full of roses. The same story is told of another royal Elizabeth, her great-aunt in Hungary, and many readers take it as a picture: charity hidden, and turned to beauty when questioned. After Denis died, Elizabeth gave herself to prayer and service beside the Poor Clares, and tradition says she died while traveling to make peace yet again.
screen: `A QUEEN IN A HARD MARRIAGE.` · `BETWEEN FATHER AND SON.` · `HER OWN BODY IN THE GAP.` · `BREAD IN THE CLOAK, THEN ROSES.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE PEACEMAKERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make peace between two people, starting here. Unclench your jaw. Bring to mind two people you know who aren't speaking, or keep clashing. Maybe you're one of them. Picture them across a room. Don't take a side. Hold each of them with the same care, as Elizabeth held a husband and a son. Ask yourself what one small, honest step toward the middle might look like. If you pray, you can hold them both before God. If you don't, simply keep them both in mind without choosing. The bell holds the time.
Elizabeth, queen of Portugal. Tradition says she rode between her husband's and her son's armies to make peace.
Your line: the peacemaker queen. Today, in one argument, at home, at work, or online, be the person who lowers the temperature instead of raising it. Day one thousand six.

howItsDone: The Church keeps an optional memorial of Saint Elizabeth of Portugal on 4 July; in Portugal, above all in Coimbra where she is buried, she is honored as the Holy Queen, and Catholics ask her prayers for peace in families and between nations.

fork.setup: you're the queen. your husband and your son have armies facing each other across a field. what do you do?
options: stay in the palace and wait for news.
ride out into the space between the armies.
back the side most likely to win.
fork.reveal: tradition says Elizabeth rode out between the two armies, and the battle was stopped before it began.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pious queen with a pretty miracle about roses.
what it means: a peacemaker who put herself between her husband and her son.
what a scholar hears: the roses legend is shared with Elizabeth of Hungary; her lasting public role was peacemaking in royal and border quarrels.

notes: Biography (princess of Aragon, married to King Denis, Denis's infidelity and her raising his children, son Afonso's revolt, riding between the armies, peacemaking with neighboring kingdoms, Poor Clares after Denis's death, dying on a peace journey): confirm each detail. 'Married young' kept vague by design (no age).
'Her greatest public work was peace': superlative; Keeper may soften to 'her best-remembered work'.
Elizabeth of Hungary as her great-aunt: commonly stated; confirm.
'On at least one occasion' rider: confirm the battle-site tradition (Alvalade).
howItsDone: burial at Coimbra and title 'Rainha Santa' (Holy Queen); confirm.
